title: Stream vs Batch Processing
tagline: Process data as it arrives, one event at a time — or wait and process it all together, later.
what_it_is: Batch processing handles data in large, scheduled chunks — e.g. processing a full day's transactions overnight. Stream processing handles data continuously, as individual events arrive, producing results in near real time.
key_points: Batch processing runs on a schedule (hourly, daily) over accumulated data — simpler to build and debug.
Stream processing runs continuously on data as it arrives, event by event or in small micro-batches.
Batch is well-suited for large-scale historical analysis where some delay is acceptable.
Streaming is required when decisions need to be made in seconds or milliseconds — fraud alerts, live dashboards.
Many modern systems use a hybrid ('Lambda' or 'Kappa' architecture) combining both batch accuracy and stream speed.
why_it_exists: Some business decisions can wait until tomorrow's report; others — like blocking a fraudulent transaction — cannot wait even a few minutes. The distinction between batch and stream processing exists because these two categories of problems have fundamentally different latency requirements and need fundamentally different tools.
intuition: Batch processing is like doing all your laundry once a week — efficient, but you might be out of clean socks for a few days. Stream processing is like washing each item the moment it gets dirty — always ready, but requires constant, ongoing effort rather than one big efficient session.
when_to_use: Use batch processing for large-scale historical reporting, ETL jobs, and analyses where near-real-time results aren't required.
Use stream processing when decisions or alerts need to happen within seconds — fraud detection, live monitoring, real-time recommendations.
when_not_to_use: Do not build a full streaming pipeline for a report that's only ever checked once a day — batch processing is simpler and cheaper.
Do not rely purely on batch processing for time-critical decisions like fraud detection, where delay has real cost.
common_mistakes: Building an unnecessarily complex streaming system for a problem that batch processing would solve just as well.
Underestimating the engineering complexity of stream processing — handling out-of-order events, late data, and exactly-once processing is genuinely hard.
Assuming streaming is strictly 'better' than batch — it trades simplicity and cost for lower latency, not a universal upgrade.
ds_usage: The choice between batch and streaming shapes the entire data architecture — from nightly ETL jobs feeding a data warehouse (batch) to Kafka-and-Spark-Streaming pipelines feeding live dashboards and fraud models (stream).
